extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory treatise guidance on (a) procedures and legal effects of reissue, surrender, disclaimer, and extension of patents and (b) doctrines defining patent infringement (making/using/selling) with illustrative cases. Focuses on statutory interpretation, commissioner powers, and equity remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patent term operates from original patent date
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is reissued, it is granted for the unexpired term, commencing from the date of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The renewed patent operates from the commencement of the original term and will enure to the benefit of assignees who became such before the reissue (even if no assignment is made after reissue). The new letters relate back to the commencement of the original term for many purposes. (See discussion and cases such as Woodworth decisions and Wilson v. Rousseau.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue may add description of subsequent improvements (historical provision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under earlier statutes the original patentee could apply to have added to the original description any new improvement of the original invention which was invented by him subsequent to the date of his patent (upon proceedings and payment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision (as described) was abrogated by the act of 1861; treat historical statutory permissions with care. The treatise cites the old act language and the required proceedings/payment; verify current law before relying on this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification in reissue subject to revision/restriction; commissioner can require disclaimer/alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an application is made for addition of a newly discovered improvement to an existing patent or when a patent is returned for correction and reissue, the specification annexed is subject to revision and restriction as in original applications; the commissioner shall not add improvements or grant reissue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification of claim in accordance with the commissioner's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commissioner has authority to require disclaimers or claim amendments as a condition of granting reissue; omissions or restrictions may be imposed by the commissioner and sanctioned by law (act of 1836/1837 cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may narrow claims in reissue (omit parts of original invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a reissue the patentee is at liberty to omit a part of his original invention if he deems it expedient, and to retain only that part of the original invention he deems fit to retain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A renewed patent that claims less than the original may be equally valid. Public policy does not prohibit such restriction because giving up part of an invention allows the public to use it; omissions may also be made to avoid misleading or unnecessarily broad language that would render the specification invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue remedies defects in specification (omitted modes/claim scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may be defective by omitting a full description of the mode of constructing a machine or by omitting to describe fully in the claim the nature, extent, and character of the invention; such defects are precisely what renewed patents are meant to remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewed patents are commonly granted to cure defects of omission in the specification or claim; courts recognize reissue to correct defects that make original specification doubtful or defective rather than utterly void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of surrender/reissue on existing injunctions and suits in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender of a patent and issuance of new letters does not necessarily defeat an injunction previously granted; in equity a bill will lie for an injunction if the patent right is admitted or well established or there is a well-grounded apprehension of intended violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable proceedings (quia timet) differ from actions at law; an existing injunction is prima facie evidence of intended violation even after reissue if patents cover same invention. Consent of assignees to surrender may affect parties' rights. Courts analyze facts and previous adjudications when deciding continuance of injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreements to assign renewed patent convey equitable title
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patentee about to apply for renewal agrees with another that, in case of success, he will assign to him the renewed patent, such an agreement is valid and conveys an equitable title which can be converted into a legal title by paying or offering to pay the stipulated consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable assignments relating to future renewed patents are recognized; practical effect depends on fulfillment of conditions and statutory/recording requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner may accept surrender and issue new letters during extended term
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissioner of patents can lawfully receive a surrender of letters-patent for a defective specification and issue new letters-patent upon an amended specification after the expiration of the term for which the original patent was granted, and pending the existence of an extended term of seven years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender and renewal may be made at any time during an extended term granted by Congress; if a new patent issued on surrender is void for causes connected with public officers' acts, the original patent might remain in force until its term expired (case law nuances apply). See Wilson v. Rousseau and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers may amend specifications for inadvertent over-breadth; effect and joinder rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertency, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is truly the patentee's own; such a disclaimer may be filed by the patentee, administrators, executors, and assigns, and thereafter is considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer cannot operate in favor of an assignee without that assignee joining in it in any suit at law or in equity. Recordation of the disclaimer is important; consult statute references (acts cited) and case law on disclaimer effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent extension statutory procedure and substantive standard (§63 act of 1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents granted prior to March 2, 1861, a patentee desiring extension must apply in writing to the commissioner stating reasons, furnish a sworn statement of the invention's ascertained value and receipts/expenditures, and file the application not more than six months nor less than ninety days before expiration; no extension can be granted after the original term expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon receipt and payment of duty, the commissioner must publish notice in Washington and other appropriate papers for at least 60 days prior to hearing, refer the case to the principal examiner for a report on patentability when originally granted, hear and decide on evidence, and grant an extension of seven years if satisfied the patentee without neglect/fault failed to obtain reasonable remuneration and that extension is just and proper considering the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's extension decision conclusive absent fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect to the entire merits of the patentee and the legal grounds for an extension, the law makes the commissioner the judge, and in the absence of fraud his adjudication is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held the commissioner's decision on extension largely conclusive; earlier boards' decisions may be limited on pure questions of law (e.g., whether an administrator could apply), but substantive adjudication on extension is generally final unless fraud is shown (cases: Clum v. Brewer; Colt v. Young).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement defined by availing oneself of the invention without sufficient variation
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement takes place whenever a party avails himself of the invention of the patentee without such variation as will constitute a new discovery; equivalently, an infringement may be a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of whether differences are immaterial or substantive is typically a question of fact for the jury or factfinder; courts compare plaintiff's and defendant's specifications and the real substance/effect of the defendants' product or process. Illustrative jury instructions and English/US case examples are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-vessel exception to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights of an American patentee do not extend to a foreign vessel lawfully entering a United States port where the improvement was placed upon her in a foreign port and authorized by the laws of the country to which she belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limited territorial exception recognized by case law (e.g., Browne v. Duchesne); analyze facts about where and under whose authority the improvement was made and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines: patent covers the machine and the mode/process of making it; making/using/selling are separate substantive infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a machine is patented, the patent covers both the machine itself and the mode or process of making it; the statute vests exclusive rights to making, using, and vending the invention, and it is therefore an infringement to make, use, or sell a patented machine even if it is not ultimately used or sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative changes clarified that each enumerated act (make, use, sell) is a substantive ground of action. Making a machine fit for use and with a design to use may be infringement; nominal damages are available if no actual loss is proved. See statutory history and cases (Whittemore v. Cutter, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere workman employed by a non-patentee is not personally liable for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere workman employed by one who is not the patentee to make parts of a patented machine is not liable for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability generally attaches to the party directing or benefiting from the infringing manufacture/use, not to ordinary laborers performing work under direction (case: Delano v. Scott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent/purpose test for making (experiment vs. infringing manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The making of a machine is an infringement when it is made for use or for sale; making for philosophical experiment or to test sufficiency of the specification may not be an infringement according to Mr. Justice Story, but other judges held motive is not a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have debated whether experimental making is exempt; the practical test often used is whether the party made the machine with intent to infringe and to deprive the patentee of lawful reward. Examine motive, commercial purpose, and whether profits are taken away from the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive use and indirect/arranged use (contracts, purchases, hiring out)
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a constructive using of a patented machine: if a person makes a machine in violation of the patentee's right or purchases it from one who made it and then hires it out, or arranges contracts to purchase the manufactured output, under some circumstances he may be held responsible for 'using' the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether contracts are real or colorable, whether the defendant owned or hired the machine, and whether the arrangements were intended to invade the patent right. A bare contract to buy output may not equal 'using' unless accompanied by ownership, hiring, or other indicia of effective control (watch-chain manufacture example).
